chapter_theme: Verses 61 to 80 each set four things in one frame (what thrives by being drawn on, what is known by what, what is better than what, what lies within a kind), so that household, learning, wealth and speech are judged by the same patterns of sign, measure and increase.

61.reading: The verse names four things that thrive by being given to: fire when ghee is sprinkled on it, the gods who grant boons when approached and praised, the milch-cow when the stall is opened for her calf to suckle, and hospitality when vessels are laid out and guests are fed well.
61.nuance: The verb நந்தும் (thrives) is repeated for fire, cow and guest-feeding, so the verse makes a single law of increase by outflow: the cow thrives by letting the calf drink, the household's hospitality by feeding. நாகர் is read here as the celestials; the verse does not say more about them.

items.claim: the fire thrives when ghee is sprinkled on it
the gods grant boons when approached and praised
the milch-cow thrives when the stall is opened and her calf is let to suckle
hospitality thrives when vessels are spread and guests are fed well

62.reading: A man's freedom from blame is to be seen in his children, his want of true friends is learned in his ruin, his prosperity is known by how his wealth moves, and by praise even those who did not esteem him are brought to esteem him.
62.nuance: கேட்டால் can be 'by ruin' (கேடு) or 'by hearing'; the reading takes ruin, which makes adversity the test of friendship. The last item breaks the 'know X by Y' pattern: புகழ்ச்சி may be one's fame or flattery offered to others, and the line does not settle which.

items.claim: a man's blamelessness is seen through his children
his lack of true friends is learned when ruin comes
his prosperity is known by the movement of his wealth
by praise even those who did not esteem him come to esteem him

63.reading: Within each kind some excel: among eyes some are dear to the one who looks, among women some are excellent without beauty of form, within a country there are good towns, and among songs there are songs that win distinction.
63.nuance: The four gems share one form (within X there are Y that excel), so worth is placed inside a class rather than given to the class. The first line is compressed; காதற்றாம் is taken as 'dear', but the clause could be read otherwise. The second item separates a woman's worth from her looks.

items.claim: among eyes, some are dear to the one who looks at them
among women, some are excellent though without beauty of form
within a country there are towns that are good
among songs there are some that attain distinction

64.reading: People worship fire seen as the flame of a wick and scorn it seen as the blaze of firewood; likewise, in one family, the world passes over the elder who grew old without learning and praises the youth of the one who learned.
64.nuance: The first two gems are one fire valued by its setting; the last two turn that image on a household, so age, like the substance of fire, does not decide worth. The ranking is inside ஒருகுடி, one family, where seniority would normally rule.

items.claim: fire as the flame of a wick is worshipped
fire as a blaze of firewood is scorned
the elder who grew old without learning is passed over
the youth of the one who learned is praised

65.reading: What the man with wealth desires comes to be, a cluster of sprouts comes from seed if there is water, a host of fortune comes if the bright red lady looks on a man, and if she is grieved it perishes.
65.nuance: ஒண்செய்யாள் is the goddess of fortune. The verse runs from wealth's power to its dependence: the rich get what they want, but the wealth itself waits on her glance, as sprouts wait on water. The fourth gem is the third reversed; one could count three things and a consequence.

items.claim: what the man with wealth desires comes to be
a cluster of sprouts comes from seed if there is water
a host of fortune comes if the bright lady looks on one
if she is grieved, the fortune perishes

66.reading: The tiger gains its sheen by eating flesh, cattle delight in the grass of wet land, all the low delight in rice from paddy, and the high delight in their own proper standing.
66.nuance: கீழ் and மேல் rank people, but the verse ranks them by what satisfies them, not by a birth rule; it states no rule of who may eat or be fed, so it carries no norm. It sets the low with the tiger and the cow as creatures pleased by food, and the high apart, pleased by வரிசை (their rank and its due).

items.claim: the tiger gains its colour by eating flesh
cattle delight in the grass of wet land
all the low delight in rice
the high delight in their own due standing

67.reading: Deeds that will recoil show it only afterward, whatever they bring, but to those who knew in advance they show it beforehand; for those who have gained things the heart is ever craving; and the deeds of those without craving do not fail.
67.nuance: The syntax of lines 1 and 2 is dense, with பின்னவாம் and முன்னவாம் played against each other; the reading is one defensible parse. The verse pairs foresight with freedom from craving as the two things that make a deed safe.

items.claim: deeds that will recoil show their result only afterward
to those who knew beforehand, such deeds show themselves in advance
the heart of those who have obtained is ever craving
the deeds of those without craving do not fail

68.reading: Those without wealth are better than those who have it and only guard it, the poor are better than those who have stored it up, those who bear are better than those who swell up and revile, and those who do not break are better than those who did.
68.nuance: Each gem is a ranking (X is better than Y), so the verse praises poverty only against hoarding, not in itself. பைத்தெழுந்து pictures the reviler rising like a cobra's spread hood. The last line is obscure: சிதையாதவர் may be those who do not ruin others or those who do not falter, and செய்தார் those who did harm or did a deed and spoiled it.

items.claim: those without wealth are better than those who have it and only guard it
the poor are better than those who have laid wealth by
those who bear are better than those who rise up and revile
those who do not break are better than those who did

69.reading: A son tells of his father's goodness, a man's face tells the desire that stands within him, one who has entered a wide well-watered field tells its nature, and the sky tells the nature of the land.
69.nuance: Every gem is a sign that discloses something hidden, so the verse is about inference: the son is evidence of the father as rain is of the land. The third item may contrast with the fourth: one learns a field by going into it, a land by its rain.

items.claim: a father's goodness is told by his son
the desire within a man is told by his face
the nature of a watered field is told by one who has entered it
the nature of the land is told by the sky

70.reading: A town is good if many live in it, a man's mind is good if he learns without fault, the sharp-horned bull gains glory by the herd of its own kind, and a family gains glory by the food it gives.
70.nuance: Two gems say what makes a thing good (நன்று) and two what gives it glory (வீறு); in each the worth comes from what surrounds or flows from it, except the mind, which is made good from within by learning.

items.claim: a town is good if many live in it
a man's mind is good if he learns without fault
the sharp-horned bull gains glory by its herd
a family gains glory by the food it gives

71.reading: A bridled horse is as its rider makes it, a man's doing of virtue is according to his strength, the width of the sluices is according to the tank that was dug, and the ways of those who live are according to their means.
71.nuance: Every gem says 'according to' (வகைய, அனைய), so virtue is measured like a horse, a sluice and a household budget. The verse does not excuse doing little; it sizes the duty to the capacity.

items.claim: a bridled horse is according to its rider
the doing of virtue is according to one's strength
the width of the sluices is according to the dug tank
the ways of those who live are according to their means

72.reading: Aeons pass reckoned by years and the night watches by naazhigai; clear understanding is found in those who are clear without delay; and the harsh delight in harsh words.
72.nuance: The first two gems say great spans are made of small units. தாழியா and தெற்றென்றார் are hard; the reading takes them as 'without delaying' and 'the clear-minded', which makes the third gem a claim that clarity shows itself at once. The last gem explains harsh speech by the speaker's nature.

items.claim: aeons pass by the count of years
the night watches pass by the naazhigai
clear understanding rests with those who are clear without delay
the harsh delight in harsh words

73.reading: If the learned man stumbles he rises again, if the unlearned fool falls his leg breaks, and, considered well, any means made with single-minded care becomes a seed that does not fail.
73.nuance: The verse counts three things, not the book's usual four: the learned man's fall, the fool's fall, and the single-minded means. The third gem gives the reason for the first two: learning is a means made with care, and so it holds when one slips.

items.claim: the learned man rises again if he stumbles
the unlearned fool breaks his leg if he falls
a means made with single-minded care becomes an unfailing seed

74.reading: Poets are like gods, those who live in one town are like kin, among kin those who cherish and serve one are like parents, and those who love the learned are like the learned.
74.nuance: Each gem lifts one group to the rank of another (gods, kin, parents, the learned), so nearness and devotion confer standing. The last gem lets the unlearned share the rank of learning through love of the learned.

items.claim: poets are like gods
those who live in one town are like kin
among kin, those who cherish and serve one are like parents
those who love the learned are like the learned

75.reading: Something is choked off the moment a lie is born, a physician names the disease the moment he is asked to speak, good people should be let go the moment they ask to leave, and the rightful heir, when he asks, should be given his share by division.
75.nuance: Every gem turns on போழ்தே (at that very moment): each act is due at once. The first line does not name what is filled in and lost when a lie is born (trust, merit or friendship); the reading leaves it open.

items.claim: the moment a lie is born, something is choked off and lost
a physician names the disease as soon as he is asked
good people should be let go as soon as they ask to leave
the rightful heir should be given his divided share when he asks

76.reading: By the tongue one knows the sweet, by smelling with the nose one knows all flowers, with the eyes one sees ornaments, and what is to be reasoned is reasoned by thought, sitting together.
76.nuance: Three senses are each matched to their own objects, and then thought (எண்ணம்) is given as a fourth faculty with its own object. தொக்கிருந்து (gathering together) makes reasoning a shared act, as in counsel, where the senses work alone.

items.claim: the tongue knows what is sweet
the nose knows all flowers by smell
the eyes see ornaments
what is to be reasoned is reasoned by thought, together

77.reading: There is no bound within which born lives do not die, no strengths that do not decline, no one who has gained unaging youth, and no one who has passed through prosperity without ruin.
77.nuance: All four gems are negations (இல்லை, இல்), so the verse is a list of things that do not exist. It draws no counsel from impermanence; it only states it.

items.claim: there is no bound within which born lives escape death
there are no strengths that do not decline
no one has gained unaging youth
no one has passed through prosperity without ruin

78.reading: A man is known by his speech, a pool by its soft water, nobility by helpfulness toward anyone, and toddy by the joy it brings to the body.
78.nuance: Each thing is known by a sign that comes out of it. Toddy closes the list without blame: the verse uses it as a plain case of a thing known by its effect, set level with nobility. யார்கண்ணும் (toward anyone at all) is what makes oppuravu a test of worth rather than favour to kin.

items.claim: a man is known by his speech
a pool is known by its soft water
nobility is known by helpfulness toward anyone
toddy is known by the joy in the body

79.reading: Is it not the tongue that cuts friendship, does not the undiscerning fool let go even when tightly bound, is not craving caught in the net of many books, and does not a resolve set amid enmity come to ruin?
79.nuance: All four gems are rhetorical questions with அன்றோ. The second and fourth lines are hard: வீங்கிப் பிணிப்பின் is read as 'though bound tight', and மாறுள் நிறுக்கும் துணிபு as a resolve weighed or set among foes. The third gem makes learning a net that catches craving.

items.claim: the tongue cuts friendship
the undiscerning fool lets go though tightly bound
craving is caught in the net of many books
a resolve set amid enmity comes to ruin

80.reading: If one gives, one should give food; if one lets go, one should let go of the hoard while life remains; if one lifts, one should lift the kin who have fallen; and if one destroys, one should destroy anger.
80.nuance: The verse is built on four conditionals (கொடுப்பின், விடுப்பின், எடுப்பின், கெடுப்பின்), each naming the best object of a verb. உயிரிடை ஈட்டை is unclear: it may be the hoard one holds while alive, or gain got from living beings; the reading takes the first.

items.claim: if one gives, food is what to give
if one lets go, the hoard held while alive is what to let go
if one lifts, the fallen among one's kin are whom to lift
if one destroys, anger is what to destroy

links.note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats the leftovers even needs sowing; the verse says hospitality thrives when vessels are spread and guests fed.
links.teaches: The couplet claims the host's field prospers without seed; the verse supplies the mechanism by analogy, since fire grows by the ghee it consumes and the cow by the milk the calf takes, so the host's outflow is itself what increases.
links.list_adds: It sets guest-feeding beside fire fed with ghee, gods given praise and a cow let to its calf, so hospitality becomes one case of a general law that things thrive by being drawn on.

links.note: Kural 62 says blameless children of good character keep evils from a parent for seven births; the verse says a man's blamelessness is seen in his children.
links.teaches: The couplet makes good children a protection for the parent and the verse makes them the evidence of the parent's worth, so read together the child both shows and secures the father's blamelessness.
links.list_adds: It puts children among four kinds of evidence (ruin for friendship, wealth's movement for prosperity), so the child becomes a sign to be read rather than a blessing to be had.

links.note: Kural 409 says the unlearned of high birth lack the worth of the learned of low birth; the verse says that in one family the learned youth is praised over the unlearned elder.
links.teaches: The couplet reverses the rank of birth for learning; the verse reverses the rank of age within a single family, so together learning overturns both of the inherited orders a household runs on.
links.list_adds: It prefaces the reversal with one fire worshipped in a lamp and scorned in firewood, so the elder and the youth are shown to be one substance valued by what it does.

links.note: Kural 84 says the fair goddess dwells gladly in the house of one who tends guests with a glad face; the verse says a host of fortune comes when the bright lady looks on one.
links.teaches: The couplet tells what keeps the goddess in a house and the verse what her look does, so together hospitality is the cause and the goddess's glance the means by which fortune gathers.
links.list_adds: It ranks her glance with water for seed and wealth for desire, then adds that her grief undoes it, so fortune is shown as conditional where the couplet shows only her staying.

links.note: Kural 167 says the fair goddess, grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister; the verse says that if the bright lady is grieved the fortune perishes.
links.teaches: The verse states only that her displeasure ruins, and the couplet names one thing that displeases her, envy, so the pair turns a bare warning into a cause and its effect.
links.list_adds: It sets the loss of fortune as the reversal of its own previous item, so the list moves from gaining to losing with one goddess at both ends.

links.note: Naladiyar 200 says the base fill themselves on rice and fried dishes a great patron gives, while to the self-reliant water won by effort is nectar; the verse says all the low delight in rice from paddy.
links.teaches: Both books define the base by being satisfied with rice, but the quatrain sets against them those who live by their own effort and the verse those who delight in their due standing, so the opposite of the base is labour in one and honour in the other.
links.list_adds: It sets the low man's rice in a series with the tiger's flesh and the cattle's grass, so appetite for food is made a creature's nature, and the high are marked off by a delight that is not eaten.

links.note: Kural 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming meet no affliction that shakes them; the verse says deeds that recoil (அதிர்க்கும்) show themselves only later, except to those who knew beforehand.
links.teaches: Both use the verb அதிர் for the shock of what comes, and the verse adds that the shock is the delayed result of one's own deed, so the couplet's foresight becomes foresight of one's own acts rather than of outside events.
links.list_adds: It joins foresight to freedom from craving in one list, so knowing beforehand and wanting nothing are set as the two guards of a deed.

links.note: Kural 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, unfailing deeds (தவாவினை) come as one wishes; the verse says the deeds of those without craving do not fail (தவாவாம்).
links.teaches: The verse repeats the couplet's promise in its own words but sets beside it that the heart of those who have gained is ever craving, which shows why the couplet's condition is hardest for the one who already has.
links.list_adds: It sets the desireless deed against the craving of those who have obtained, a contrast between two kinds of person that the couplet, which speaks of one, lacks.

links.note: Kural 228 asks whether hard-eyed hoarders who keep and lose do not know the joy of giving; the verse ranks those without wealth above those who have it and only guard it.
links.teaches: The couplet says the hoarder misses a joy; the verse goes further and ranks him below the man who has nothing, so wealth kept unused is shown to be worse than poverty, not merely less than giving.
links.list_adds: It frames the point as a ranking and repeats it with the poor over the hoarder, then sets forbearance over reviling in the same form, so hoarding is placed among vices of the same weight as abuse.

links.note: Kural 159 says those who bear the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers; the verse ranks those who bear above those who rise up and revile.
links.teaches: The couplet measures the forbearer upward against the renouncer and the verse measures him against the reviler beside him, so forbearance is placed both by its reward and by the act it refuses.
links.list_adds: It sets forbearance in a series of 'better than' rankings with poverty over hoarding, so restraint of anger and restraint of possession are judged by one standard.

links.note: Kural 706 says the face shows what is strongest in the heart, as crystal shows what is near it; the verse says a man's face tells the desire within him.
links.teaches: The couplet says the face shows whatever is strongest and the verse names that thing as desire (வேட்கை), so the pair makes the face chiefly a betrayer of wants.
links.list_adds: It ranks the face with a son revealing his father and rain revealing a land, so the face becomes one case of reading a hidden source from its outflow.

links.note: Kural 70 says the son's help to his father is that people ask what penance his father did; the verse says a son tells of his father's goodness.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the praise a debt the son repays; the verse states it as a fact of inference, so read together the son repays his father by being the evidence others read.
links.list_adds: It places the son among natural signs (the face, the field, the sky), so the father's repute is shown to be inferred as surely as rain is from cloud.

links.note: Thirikadugam 10 says a town without teachers yields no good; the verse says a town is good if many live in it.
links.teaches: The verse makes a town good by its numbers and Thirikadugam makes it worthless without teachers, so the pair shows the group measuring a town both by size and by learning, and a populous town can still fail the second test.

links.note: Kural 83 says the life of one who tends guests daily does not fall into ruin; the verse says a family gains glory by the food it gives.
links.teaches: The couplet answers the fear that giving food ruins a house; the verse claims more, that it is the source of the family's distinction, so feeding is shown as both safe and the very thing that ranks a house.
links.list_adds: It ranks the family's food-giving with a bull's herd and a town's people, so a house's glory is made to come from those it sustains.

links.note: Kural 33 tells one to do virtue without stopping as far as one is able; the verse says the doing of virtue is according to one's strength.
links.teaches: The couplet uses capacity as a floor (do all you can) and the verse uses it as a measure (each gives by his strength), so read together capacity both limits what is owed and forbids doing less.
links.list_adds: It sets virtue with a rider's horse, a tank's sluices and a household's spending, so the measure by capacity becomes a principle of proportion across unlike things.

links.note: Kural 478 says there is no ruin if the outflow is not wider than the inflow, using the image of channels; the verse says sluices are as wide as the dug tank and people live according to their means.
links.teaches: Both picture a household as water and channels, and the verse adds that the outlet should be cut to the size of the tank, so the couplet's rule of balance becomes a rule of construction made when the tank is dug.
links.list_adds: It sets the sluice beside the measure of virtue by strength, so spending and doing good are governed by the same proportion.

links.note: Kural 99 asks why one who sees the good of sweet speech would use harsh words; the verse says the harsh delight in harsh words.
links.teaches: The couplet's question assumes harsh speech is a mistake; the verse answers that it is a pleasure to the harsh, so the pair shows that reasoning against harsh words will not reach those whose nature enjoys them.
links.list_adds: It places harsh speech after units of time and the clear-minded, so a speaker's words are shown as following from his nature as watches follow from naazhigai.

links.note: Kural 415 says the words of the good are like a staff on slippery ground; the verse says the learned man rises if he stumbles while the fool breaks his leg.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the staff to the hearer as another's words; the verse puts the support inside the learned man himself, so learning is shown as the staff once it has been taken in.
links.list_adds: It sets the learned and the fool side by side in the same fall and then names the cause, a means made with single-minded care, which the couplet's image does not explain.

links.note: Kural 410 says others are to the learned as beasts are to people; the verse says those who love the learned are like the learned.
links.teaches: The couplet draws a line between the learned and all others; the verse lets those who love the learned cross it, so the pair shows the divide is passable through devotion rather than study alone.
links.list_adds: It closes a list in which each group is lifted to the rank of another (poets to gods, townsfolk to kin, servers to parents), so loving the learned becomes one of several ways nearness confers rank.

links.note: Kural 27 says the world lies with one who discerns the five sense-kinds; the verse names three senses with their objects and then thought.
links.teaches: The couplet ends its list at the five senses; the verse adds thought as a further faculty with its own object, done in company, so the pair shows the ethics group placing counsel beyond the discernment of sense.
links.list_adds: It pairs each faculty with its object and makes the last one collective (தொக்கிருந்து), a step from individual sensing to shared deliberation that the couplet lacks.

links.note: Naladiyar 2 says wealth turns like a cart wheel and urges sharing its food at once; the verse says no one has passed through prosperity without ruin.
links.teaches: The quatrain draws a counsel of giving from wealth's turning and the verse draws none, so set together they show the same observation used once as an argument and once as a bare fact.
links.list_adds: It compresses the impermanence of life, strength, youth and wealth into four negations in one verse, where the Naladiyar gives them separate chapters.

links.note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood knowing grey hair would come; the verse says no one has gained unaging youth.
links.teaches: The quatrain turns the loss of youth into a reason to renounce early; the verse states only that the loss is universal, so the pair shows the Naladiyar's renunciation resting on a premise the other book states without that conclusion.
links.list_adds: It sets youth among strength, life and wealth, all lost alike, so the loss of youth is not singled out as the Naladiyar's chapter makes it.

links.note: Kural 986 says the touchstone of worth is accepting defeat even from those not one's equal; the verse says nobility is known by helpfulness toward anyone.
links.teaches: Both make the test of worth one's conduct toward those who are no match for one (துலையல்லார், யார்கண்ணும்), the couplet by yielding and the verse by helping, so the pair shows nobility tested where nothing is owed.
links.list_adds: It sets the sign of nobility with the signs of a man, a pool and toddy, so worth is known by its outflow as a pool by its water.

links.note: Kural 127 says whatever else one fails to guard one should guard the tongue; the verse says the tongue cuts friendship.
links.teaches: The couplet warns of the suffering an unguarded tongue brings to its owner; the verse names a particular loss, friendship, so the pair shows what is at stake in the couplet's general warning.
links.list_adds: It sets the tongue beside the fool who lets go and the resolve that fails, so speech is listed among the things that break bonds.

links.note: Kural 303 says to forget anger toward anyone, since evils are born from it; the verse says that if one destroys anything, it should be anger.
links.teaches: The couplet asks for anger to be let go of; the verse turns destruction itself toward anger, so the pair shows the same urge to destroy being redirected rather than given up.
links.list_adds: It frames each counsel as the best object of a verb (give food, lift fallen kin, destroy anger), so the destructive impulse is given a proper target like the giving and the lifting.

links.note: Kural 226 says relieving the destroying hunger of the destitute is where one with wealth should store it; the verse says that if one gives, one should give food.
links.teaches: The couplet says where wealth is best stored and the verse which gift is best, so together food given to the hungry is both the best gift and the safest store.
links.list_adds: It ranks food first among gifts by setting giving beside letting go, lifting and destroying, each with its one right object.

source_issues: 71 line 2: the text has ஆற்றல் வகைய வறஞ்செய்கை and தொட்ட (line 2); the tamilvu text reads அறம் செயல் and தோட்ட. The reading does not turn on the difference.
66 lines 2-3: இன்புறூங்உங் is an odd spelling, probably for இன்புறூஉம்; it appears twice.
